meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Folks are usually about as happy as they make up their minds to be'?
meta.ogDescription: No evidence Lincoln said it. Earliest trace: a 1914 Frank Crane column crediting him with no source. Carnegie and Disney's Pollyanna did the rest.

answer.label: Not Abraham Lincoln — no evidence he said it
answer.sourceLine: There is no substantive evidence that Lincoln ever said or wrote this. The earliest documented appearance is a column by Dr. Frank Crane on 1 January 1914 — roughly fifty years after Lincoln’s death — which credited “Lincoln’s saying” but gave no source, and Crane himself printed at least three different wordings over the years. It spread through Orison Swett Marden, Dale Carnegie’s How to Win Friends and Influence People (1936), and Disney’s Pollyanna (1960).

source.excerpt: Folks are usually about as happy as they make up their minds to be.
trail: Quote Investigator traced the earliest instance to a New Year’s Resolutions column by Dr. Frank Crane on 1 January 1914, which referred to “Lincoln’s saying that folks are usually about as happy as they make up their minds to be.”

Crane printed at least three different phrasings between 1914 and 1920, and never cited where in Lincoln he found it — a hallmark of an attribution invented rather than documented, per Quote Investigator.

The saying reached a mass audience through Dale Carnegie’s 1936 bestseller and Disney’s 1960 film Pollyanna, both of which credited it to Lincoln, cementing a misattribution with no primary basis (Quote Investigator).
source.excerptNote: Frank Crane’s 1914 wording. He later reworked it — “most people in this world are about as happy as they have made up their minds to be” (1916) and “a man is usually about as happy as he has made up his mind to be” (1920) — a fluidity that argues against a fixed Lincoln original.
source.rightsNote: The earliest documented wording appears in Frank Crane’s newspaper column of 1 January 1914 — well before the 1931 U.S. public-domain cutoff — and short aphorisms are not themselves copyrightable, so the text carries no active rights claim. It is not a work of Abraham Lincoln.

author.name: Abraham Lincoln
author.heading: Why it lands on Lincoln
author.bio: Abraham Lincoln (1809–1865) led the United States through the Civil War and is among the most quoted figures in American history. That fame makes him one of the internet’s biggest magnets for feel-good sayings he never spoke — his documented words survive in speeches, letters, and the Collected Works, and this cheerful aphorism appears in none of them. The line was attached to his name only in the twentieth century, long after his death.

misattribution.heading: Who really said it
misattribution.intro: This is a textbook twentieth-century misattribution: a cheerful, self-help-friendly line pinned on Lincoln decades after his death, with no trace in anything he actually wrote or spoke.

items.why: No instance of this saying appears in Lincoln’s documented speeches, letters, or the Collected Works. Quote Investigator concludes there is “no substantive evidence” he used the expression.

Columnist Frank Crane put the line in print on 1 January 1914, attributing it to Lincoln but supplying no source — and he rephrased it repeatedly in later years, which is inconsistent with quoting a fixed original (Quote Investigator).
Carnegie’s How to Win Friends and Influence People (1936) and the 1960 Disney film Pollyanna both credited Lincoln, carrying the misattribution to millions (Quote Investigator).

misattribution.truthLine: Best evidence: a modern maxim mis-credited to Lincoln, first documented in a 1914 Frank Crane column and popularized by Carnegie and Disney — not the words of Abraham Lincoln (Quote Investigator).

context.heading: Why it stuck to Lincoln
lead: Lincoln’s stature makes his name a magnet for uplifting sayings, and this one had powerful twentieth-century amplifiers. Once Frank Crane credited “Lincoln’s saying” in 1914, the attribution was picked up by motivational writers, then hard-wired into popular culture by Dale Carnegie’s runaway 1936 bestseller and Disney’s beloved 1960 film Pollyanna.
The result is a line that sounds like folk-wisdom Lincoln, but is really an early self-help aphorism searching for a distinguished author.
context.pull: First documented in 1914 — roughly fifty years after Lincoln died.
